answer: I'd like to talk about something I own that is closely connected to where I come from. A traditional handmade item I own and treasure is a beautifully woven shawl made by artisans in a rural part of my country. In fact, it was woven on a handloom in a village near Sirajganj, an area well known for its weaving. It was given to me by my grandmother, who bought it from a weaver she has known for years, and it is a wonderful example of local [[craftsmanship]]. What makes it special is that it was made entirely by hand, using techniques passed down through generations. The intricate patterns and vivid colours are genuinely [[exquisite]], and no two pieces are ever exactly alike. Mine is a deep maroon with a fine cream border, and if you look closely you can see tiny irregularities that show a human being made it. I use it mainly during the cooler months, and it always draws compliments. I wrap it around my shoulders on foggy winter mornings, and I also wear it to weddings and family gatherings, because it looks smart over a panjabi. Beyond its practical use, I value it because it represents a fading [[heritage]] that deserves to be preserved. In a world dominated by mass-produced goods, owning something so [[authentic]] feels increasingly meaningful. Honestly, I feel a sense of responsibility to look after it well. It connects me to my culture, to my grandmother and to the skilled hands that created it. I think items like this are far more valuable than anything [[churned out]] by a factory.

followUps.q: Do many young people in Bangladesh wear handmade clothes?
followUps.answer: Fewer than before, sadly, although handloom fabrics are becoming fashionable again among some young people. Social media has helped, because small weavers can now sell directly to customers.

followUps.q: Would you buy another handmade item?
followUps.answer: Definitely. Next time I visit my grandparents, I'd like to buy a couple of handwoven gamchhas from the local weavers, both to use and to support their [[livelihoods]].

note: Made the giver his (living) grandmother and located the weaving near Sirajganj's handloom villages; added description and when he wears it; new mark 'churned out'.
